C1.text: The actual split of chores explains only a small part of the variation in a partner's perceived fairness.
C1.reading: Whole-model variance explained is small (about 5% to 19% in the studies that report it, and at most 20% in most studies the review cites), so the actual split explains a small part of a partner's perceived fairness; no study reports the split's own share, and its slope can still be steep.

C2.text: Comparison referents predict a partner's perceived fairness after the actual split is accounted for.
C2.reading: Weakly supported: one Italian survey finds referents predict a partner's perceived fairness net of the split for male referents only, with self-serving referent choice suspected; the reviews report only zero-order associations and the direction is undetermined.

C3.text: The justifications a partner accepts for an unequal split predict that partner's perceived fairness after the actual split is accounted for.
C3.reading: Open: no paper read in full tests accepted justifications against perceived fairness net of the split; the nearest evidence is that a partner's voice in how chores are divided predicts it, and a reduced-employment justification did not work in one Swedish study.

C4.text: A partner's perceived fairness is more strongly associated with that partner's relationship satisfaction than the actual split is.
C4.reading: Probably true on average, mostly for women: fairness outranks the split in the pooled models of three studies and in the reviews, but it reverses for Jewish women, for men in one study and for working-class wives, and no study tests the difference on a common scale.

C5.text: The association between the actual split and relationship satisfaction is mediated by perceived fairness.
C5.reading: Partly supported for women (Connecticut, pooled Israeli women) and not for men; the mediation tests are cross-sectional coefficient comparisons with no time ordering, and the review says little systematic study exists.

C6.text: Each partner over-claims their own contribution: the two partners' self-reported shares of chores sum to more than the whole.
C6.reading: Supported in direction by three dyadic studies: partners' shares sum above the whole by a few percentage points (4.67 of 150 units in 1979 couples; 103.9% overall and 107.0% for cognitive labour in 235 UK couples); chores-only evidence is thin and two samples show no excess.

C7.text: Which chores a partner does predicts that partner's perceived fairness beyond the time the chores take.
C7.reading: Open: no paper read in full separates which chores a partner does from the time they take; the reviews report from other studies that female-typed chores predict perceived fairness best, by comparison of correlations only.

C8.text: Studies measure perceived fairness of the division of chores mainly with a single self-report item.
C8.reading: Supported: Mikula's review says the one-item NSFH fairness measure underlies most recent studies, and ten of twelve primary studies read in full use one self-report item; the exceptions are a two-item and a nine-item measure, and item wording differs.

C9.text: A partner who is over-benefited by the allocation reports lower relationship satisfaction than a partner in an equitable allocation.
C9.reading: Little evidence, mixed: one US survey finds no satisfaction penalty for an over-benefited partner on chores, one German panel finds one for doing a bit less than a fair share, two others find similar quality or a null, and four studies cannot test it.
